1.stem: [Academic Talk — Paleoclimatology] How does the professor respond to the claim that the cooling event was hemispheric rather than a purely regional effect?

options.A: She doubts it -- a fen on another continent shows no matching signal at all
options.B: She accepts it, mainly because the timing matches a known cooling signal recorded elsewhere in the hemisphere
options.C: She rejects a hemispheric cause but allows a wider regional footprint than first thought
options.D: She thinks it's unresolved, since too few other sites have been sampled at this resolution

2.stem: [Academic Talk — Chronobiology] How does the professor respond to the claim that the rhythm shift tracks temperature rather than light exposure?

options.A: She rejects temperature as the driver but allows it may set the pace within a season
options.B: She accepts it, mainly because burrow temperature logs track the shift almost exactly
options.C: She doubts it -- the shift happens on the same calendar date regardless of that year's weather
options.D: She thinks the two explanations can't be separated with the equipment currently in use

3.stem: [Academic Talk — Ethnobotany] What does the professor imply the ethnobotany team will do with the community's own oral history recordings?

options.A: Count how many independent tellings mention the same secondary plant used alongside it
options.B: Compare preparation methods described across three generations of recordings
options.C: Time-stamp each recording against the community's own seasonal calendar
options.D: Note which recordings mention harvesting the plant only at a particular moon phase

4.stem: [Academic Talk — Paleoclimatology] Why does the professor mention the peat-cutter's account from the 1880s?

options.A: It describes a buried layer of ash, though the account gives no indication of its thickness
options.B: It preserves a plant name no longer used by botanists today
options.C: It records the fen's water level dropping enough to cut new ground
options.D: It notes finding old timber the team later cored for its own record

5.stem: [Academic Talk — Selenography] What does the professor imply the digitisation project will do with the atlas's original glass plates?

options.A: Compare plate glass thickness against the atlas's own printed specifications
options.B: Scan them at a resolution well beyond what the printed atlas ever showed
options.C: Photograph the plates' handwritten edge labels for a searchable index
options.D: Cross-reference the plate numbers against the maker's private notebook

6.stem: [Academic Talk — Phenology] Why does the professor mention a Victorian diary entry from the 1860s?

options.A: It describes a flower now absent from the site entirely
options.B: It gives the earliest specific bloom date on record for the site
options.C: It records a bloom failure the current team can't otherwise explain
options.D: It notes a specific week when frost damaged that year's early flowers

7.stem: [Academic Talk — Toxicology] What does the professor say the sediment cores from Ferrow Creek showed about toxin concentration over the last decade?

options.A: It rose steadily each year, with no year showing a decline
options.B: It stayed essentially flat, with only minor year-to-year noise
options.C: It spiked twice, a decade apart, then returned to baseline both times
options.D: It declined for years, then rose sharply in the most recent samples

8.stem: [Academic Talk — Metrology] What does the professor say the guild's ledger recorded about disputes over short measure?

options.A: Complaints were rare, and mostly involved cloth rather than grain
options.B: Complaints dropped sharply after the guild introduced a public checking table
options.C: Complaints spiked in years when grain prices were highest
options.D: Complaints came almost entirely from one trading family

9.stem: [Academic Talk — Metrology] How does the professor respond to the claim that the rod itself shrank over the centuries, rather than always having been slightly short?

options.A: She rejects shrinkage but allows a later repair may have shortened it slightly
options.B: She doubts it -- bronze rods of this alloy don't contract measurably at room temperature
options.C: She accepts it, pointing to a slow contraction rate documented in similar bronze rods
options.D: She thinks it's undecidable without a rod of known, unworn original length to compare

10.stem: [Academic Talk — Hydrology] How does the professor respond to the claim that the reservoir, not the drought, explains the drop in downstream flow?

options.A: She thinks it can't be separated yet, since the drought and the reservoir's opening happened in the same year
options.B: She accepts it, mainly because releases have stayed below the flow the drought alone would predict
options.C: She doubts it -- a nearby stream with no reservoir shows nearly the same drop
options.D: She rejects the reservoir explanation but allows its releases have made a bad drought slightly worse

11.stem: [Academic Talk — Metrology] Why does the professor mention the guild's old inspection stamps?

options.A: One surviving stamp shows heavier use than the others, suggesting it covered the busiest part of town
options.B: Their design changed once, marking a shift in who ran inspections
options.C: Their wear pattern shows which merchants were checked most often
options.D: They were applied to barrel staves, not to the length rods themselves

12.stem: [Academic Talk — Hydrology] What does the professor say the streamflow gauges below Coldrun Gap recorded in the two years after the reservoir opened?

options.A: Flow dropped gradually across both years, with no sign of recovery
options.B: Flow rose in the first year before dropping in the second
options.C: Flow dropped sharply in the first year, then partly recovered in the second
options.D: Flow dropped in both years, but far less than the operator's own model predicted

13.stem: [Academic Talk — Phenology] How does the professor respond to the claim that the earlier blooming is driven by reduced grazing rather than spring warmth?

options.A: She accepts it, pointing to ungrazed plots blooming earliest within the same spring
options.B: She thinks the two factors can't be cleanly separated with the plots currently monitored
options.C: She rejects grazing as the driver but allows it may account for a few especially early years
options.D: She doubts it -- the trend continues even in plots that have never been grazed

14.stem: [Academic Talk — Selenography] What does the professor say the observatory's nightly logs recorded about the atlas maker's viewing conditions?

options.A: Conditions were logged as average on most nights, with few extremes either way
options.B: Poor seeing was blamed for nearly a third of all missed nights
options.C: The best results came from a handful of exceptionally still winter nights
options.D: Most productive nights came in a narrow window each autumn

15.stem: [Academic Talk — Chronobiology] What does the professor say the activity loggers recorded about the voles' burrow-emergence times across the study?

options.A: Emergence shifted earlier for several years, then partly reverted in the two most recent seasons
options.B: Emergence grew steadily later, reversing only in the final season
options.C: Emergence grew steadily earlier across the whole study period
options.D: Emergence shifted abruptly in one season, then held steady after

16.stem: [Academic Talk — Paleoclimatology] What does the professor say the pollen counts from Sedge Fen showed about tree cover during the cooling event?

options.A: Tree pollen barely changed, while grass pollen rose instead
options.B: Tree pollen dropped, recovered, then dropped again within the event
options.C: Tree pollen dropped sharply within a single decade of sediment
options.D: Tree pollen declined gradually across more than a century

17.stem: [Academic Talk — Toxicology] What does the professor imply the team will do with the new field bioassay kit?

options.A: Recalibrate it against a certified reference sample before the season starts
options.B: Use it to screen samples from three creeks the lab has never covered
options.C: Deploy it at two additional depths within the same monitoring station
options.D: Run it alongside the lab assay for one season to check the two agree

18.stem: [Academic Talk — Phenology] What does the professor say the volunteer record showed about the bluebell's first-bloom date at Thorne Vale?

options.A: It advanced gradually at first, then accelerated in the record's final third
options.B: It has advanced by roughly two weeks over the record's length
options.C: It advanced sharply, then plateaued for the record's final third
options.D: It has advanced overall, but in fits and starts, with the biggest jumps in drought years

19.stem: [Academic Talk — Selenography] Why does the professor mention the correspondence with a rival observatory?

options.A: It shows the rival reached the same crater count independently
options.B: It dates when the two observatories agreed to share plates
options.C: It preserves a disagreement over naming rights for one crater
options.D: It records an early, private admission that the printed atlas undercounted a nearby cluster of small craters

20.stem: [Academic Talk — Toxicology] How does the professor respond to the claim that the toxin comes from upstream mine tailings rather than a natural algae bloom?

options.A: She rejects the tailings explanation but allows a smaller natural source may compound it
options.B: She accepts it, mainly because the toxin's chemical signature matches known tailings compounds
options.C: She thinks the question is still open, since neither source has been ruled out by testing so far
options.D: She doubts it -- the tailings pond drains a different sub-basin entirely

21.stem: [Academic Talk — Chronobiology] Why does the professor mention the trapping ledger kept by a local naturalist in the 1970s?

options.A: It records emergence times decades before any logger existed
options.B: It notes a vole population crash the current team can't otherwise explain
options.C: It fixes the date the hollow was first cleared of undergrowth
options.D: It documents a predator no longer found on the site

22.stem: [Academic Talk — Ethnobotany] What does the professor say the herbarium specimen labels from the 1930s recorded about where the plant was collected?

options.A: Specimens came mostly from gardens, not the wild marsh population
options.B: Nearly all specimens came from a single, small stretch of the marsh
options.C: Specimens were collected from the marsh in only two of the recorded years
options.D: Specimens came from scattered sites across the whole marsh

23.stem: [Academic Talk — Chronobiology] What does the professor imply the team will do with the rhythm data once this season ends?

options.A: Share the raw logger data with a lab studying a related burrowing species
options.B: Cross-tabulate the rhythm data against moon-phase records for the same nights
options.C: Compare it against a nearby group of voles living without any artificial light nearby
options.D: Re-run the analysis excluding the two loggers that failed mid-season

24.stem: [Academic Talk — Phenology] What does the professor imply the phenology project will do with this year's volunteer submissions?

options.A: Flag submissions from sites the record has covered for under five years
options.B: Tabulate them by postcode to check for geographic clustering
options.C: Map them against soil-temperature sensors installed for the first time this year
options.D: Weight submissions from more experienced volunteers more heavily in the final analysis

25.stem: [Academic Talk — Selenography] How does the professor respond to the claim that a particular crater was drawn in the wrong position deliberately, to support the maker's own theory, rather than by honest error?

options.A: She doubts it -- the same small offset appears in three unrelated formations, suggesting a lens error
options.B: She accepts it, since the position change would have neatly supported his published theory
options.C: She rejects deliberate placement but allows the maker rushed that plate under deadline
options.D: She thinks it can't be settled from the atlas alone, since the plate for that region is lost

26.stem: [Academic Talk — Paleoclimatology] What does the professor imply the team will do with the newly identified ash layer?

options.A: Use its depth to check whether the fen's sediment has compacted evenly
options.B: Match its chemistry to a known eruption to pin down an exact date
options.C: Send a sample for an independent lab to confirm the composition
options.D: Search two other regional fens for the same layer

27.stem: [Academic Talk — Toxicology] Why does the professor mention the cannery's shipping manifests from the 1950s?

options.A: They record a batch of fish rejected for an unusual smell
options.B: They list a fine the cannery paid for a discharge violation
options.C: They document a change in where the cannery sourced its catch
options.D: They show the cannery closed years before anyone suspected contamination

28.stem: [Academic Talk — Metrology] What does the professor imply the recalibration team will do with the recovered Harrow ell rod?

options.A: X-ray it for an internal seam that might explain its length
options.B: Measure it at three points along its length to check for a consistent taper
options.C: Cut a small cross-section from the rod's decorative end cap for material dating
options.D: Compare it against a rod from a neighbouring town's guild archive

29.stem: [Academic Talk — Ethnobotany] How does the professor respond to the claim that the plant-use practice was introduced by traders rather than developed locally?

options.A: She thinks it's unresolved, since both regions could have developed similar methods independently
options.B: She accepts it, mainly because the preparation method matches one documented in a trading-partner region
options.C: She doubts it -- the practice uses a local plant part no trading-region method touches at all
options.D: She rejects outside introduction but allows traders may have spread the practice to nearby communities

30.stem: [Academic Talk — Hydrology] Why does the professor mention the old mill's water-rights record from the 1890s?

options.A: It sets a legal minimum flow the reservoir must maintain downstream
options.B: It records a much larger historical flow than any modern gauge has seen
options.C: It documents a dispute over water rights between two now-vanished mills
options.D: It fixes the date the mill itself stopped operating

31.stem: [Academic Talk — Ethnobotany] Why does the professor mention an early missionary's journal from the 1750s?

options.A: It notes trade goods passing through the area at the time
options.B: It's the earliest written record of the community using the plant medicinally
options.C: It preserves a place name for the marsh no longer in local use
options.D: It records a plague the missionary blamed on the marsh's water

32.stem: [Academic Talk — Hydrology] What does the professor imply the streamflow team will do to separate the reservoir's effect from the drought's?

options.A: Install a new gauge just above the reservoir to isolate its inflow
options.B: Pull satellite soil-moisture data for the whole watershed to check drought severity independently
options.C: Model what flow would have looked like without the reservoir, using rainfall records
options.D: Ask the reservoir operator for its gate-opening logs instead of relying on downstream gauges
